# Skill Author

Helps you write **new agent skills** that follow the best-practices documented at
https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/ — without you having to re-read those pages
every time. Pairs with `skill-creator` (which handles eval/iterate/optimize loops
once a draft exists).

## When to use this vs `skill-creator`

| Task | Use |
|---|---|
| "I want to make a new skill for X" | **skill-author** (scaffold + author) |
| "Scaffold the SKILL.md / a reference / a script" | **skill-author** |
| "Lint this skill draft" | **skill-author** |
| "My skill isn't triggering when I want it to" | `skill-creator` (description optimization) |
| "Run test cases against my skill, benchmark it" | `skill-creator` (eval loop) |
| "Compare two versions of my skill" | `skill-creator` (blind comparison) |

If both apply, start here, then hand off to `skill-creator` once the draft is solid.

## Workflow

### 1. Capture intent (1 minute)

Before scaffolding, get four answers — usually just by asking the user:

1. **What does it do?** (one sentence)
2. **When should it trigger?** (specific user phrases / contexts)
3. **What does it output?** (file, command result, plan, prose)
4. **Is the output objectively verifiable?** (decides whether `skill-creator` evals are worth the effort later)

Write these four down before touching files. They become the seeds for the
description, the workflow body, and the future eval set.

### 2. Scaffold

Use `scripts/new-skill.sh` to produce the directory layout. The script
auto-detects **scope** (where to put the skill) and fans out discovery
symlinks for non-universal agents so the skill is loadable immediately.

```bash
bash skills/local/skill-author/scripts/new-skill.sh <skill-name>
```

Three scopes (auto-detected; override with `--local` / `--project` / `--global`):

| Scope | Canonical dir | Symlinks created |
|---|---|---|
| **LOCAL** (this publishing repo: vendor.yaml / skills/local/ found walking up) | `<repo>/skills/local/<name>/` (or `skills/vendor/<name>/` with `--vendor`) | `.agents/skills/<name>` + `.claude/skills/<name>` -> `../../skills/{local,vendor}/<name>` |
| **PROJECT** (inside another git repo) | `<repo>/.agents/skills/<name>/` (universal agents — Cursor / Codex / OpenCode / Warp — pick this up directly) | `.claude/skills/<name>` -> `../../.agents/skills/<name>` (+ any already-present non-universal agent dir at the repo root) |
| **GLOBAL** (no git repo found) | `~/.agents/skills/<name>/` | `~/.claude/skills/<name>` -> `../../.agents/skills/<name>` (+ any detected non-universal agent dir under `$HOME`) |

The template's frontmatter has placeholders that lint will reject — this is on
purpose so the agent can't forget to fill them in.

> **Important**: When the user's intent is ambiguous (they're inside a git repo
> but haven't said whether the skill should live with the project or be
> available everywhere), **ask** "system-wide (`--global`) or just this
> project (`--project`)?" before running the script. The script is
> non-interactive — once you've picked a scope, files land and symlinks fan
> out without further prompting.

After running, the script emits a single JSON object on stdout with
`{skill, mode, canonical, symlinks[], next_steps[]}` so you can chain
follow-up actions deterministically.

### 3. Author the SKILL.md

Read `references/authoring-patterns.md` before writing the body. The patterns
that matter most:

- **Description must be "pushy"** and include concrete trigger contexts. Naive
  descriptions cause undertriggering — the #1 failure mode of new skills. Keep
  this within the cross-agent budget: 120-500 chars is the preferred range,
  501-900 is valid but context-heavy, 901-1024 is valid but close to hard
  loader limits, and >1024 is invalid for Codex/Cursor/spec-aligned skills.
- **Gotchas section** — environment-specific facts that defy reasonable
  assumptions. The single highest-value section in most skills.
- **Output templates** — agents pattern-match against concrete structures more
  reliably than they follow prose descriptions of formats.
- **Calibrated specificity** — be prescriptive only where the task is fragile;
  give the agent freedom (and explain *why*) where multiple approaches are valid.
- **Defaults, not menus** — pick one tool/approach and mention alternatives as
  escape hatches.

Keep `SKILL.md` under 500 lines. If you blow past that, move detail into
`references/<topic>.md` and tell the agent **when** to load it ("Read X if Y
happens"), not just that it exists.

### 4. Design any scripts

Before writing a script, read `references/script-design.md`. Skills script
design is meaningfully different from "regular" CLI script design because the
caller is an LLM reading your stderr to decide what to do next. The non-obvious
requirements:

- No interactive prompts, ever (agents run in non-interactive shells)
- `--help` is the primary interface documentation — keep it concise but complete
- Errors must say *what was expected* and *what to try*, not just *what failed*
- Structured stdout (JSON/CSV/TSV), prose diagnostics to stderr — separate them
- `--dry-run` for any destructive operation
- Pin versions for `uvx` / `npx` / `pipx` invocations

For Python helpers, prefer **PEP 723 inline dependencies** + `uv run` over
`requirements.txt` — the script becomes self-contained and the agent doesn't
have to set up an environment first.

### 5. Lint

Run the linter before committing or handing off to `skill-creator`:

```bash
bash skills/local/skill-author/scripts/lint-skill.sh skills/local/<skill-name>
```

It checks three things:

1. **Frontmatter & length** — `name` and `description` exist; name is
   hyphen-case and <=64 chars; description has a "use when" trigger phrase,
   respects the 1024-char hard limit, and SKILL.md is under 500 lines.
2. **Script hygiene** — every `scripts/*.sh` has a shebang, is executable, and
   responds to `--help` (presence of the flag handler, not necessarily a working
   script).
3. **Reference reachability** — every file in `references/` is mentioned at
   least once from `SKILL.md` (no dead reference docs).

Fix every error. Warnings are advisory but usually worth addressing.

### 6. (Optional) Hand off to skill-creator

Once lint [REDACTED:generic-credential-uri]es and the skill *looks* right, the next questions are
quantitative: does it trigger reliably? does it produce good output? That's
`skill-creator` territory. Tell the user: "skill-author got the structure
right. If you want to validate it works on real prompts, the `skill-creator`
skill runs test cases and benchmarks."

## Available scripts

- **`scripts/new-skill.sh <name>`** — Scaffold the canonical skill dir
  (SKILL.md, references/, scripts/, assets/) and add discovery symlinks for
  non-universal agents. Auto-detects scope (LOCAL / PROJECT / GLOBAL); see
  table in step 2.
  - Scope flags (mutually exclusive): `--local` (force this repo's
    `skills/local/`), `--project` (force `<repo>/.agents/skills/`),
    `--global` (force `~/.agents/skills/`).
  - Other flags: `--vendor` (LOCAL only — `skills/vendor/<name>/` instead of
    `skills/local/`; rare, vendored skills normally come via `vendor.yaml`);
    `--root DIR` (override walk-up); `--no-symlinks` (skip the fan-out);
    `--dry-run`; `--force` (overwrite existing canonical dir + replace
    symlinks).
- **`scripts/lint-skill.sh <skill-dir>`** — Run frontmatter, script hygiene,
  and reference reachability checks. Exit non-zero on any error.
  - Flags: `--strict` (treat warnings as errors); `--quiet` (only print failures).
- **`scripts/lint-frontmatter.sh [PATH...]`** — YAML-parse the frontmatter of
  every `SKILL.md` under PATH (default `.`) with a real parser, and check that
  the root is a mapping with string `name` + `description`. Catches the
  breakage class `lint-skill.sh`'s awk extractor cannot see — an unquoted
  `description:` containing `": "` makes `npx skills` (and Claude Code /
  Cursor) **silently skip the skill**. `lint-skill.sh` calls this for the
  single-skill case; run it directly to sweep a whole collection.
  - Flags: `--parser auto|yq|python3|node` (`node` = the js `yaml` package,
    exactly what `npx skills` uses); `--quiet`.

## Bundled assets

Templates that `new-skill.sh` copies and that you can reference manually:

- `assets/SKILL.md.template` — Frontmatter + workflow skeleton with placeholders.
- `assets/reference.md.template` — Reference doc skeleton (TOC + sections).
- `assets/script-bash.template` — Bash 3.2 compatible script with `set -euo pipefail`,
  `--help` / `--dry-run` flag handler, structured-output friendly logging
  (data → stdout, prose → stderr).
- `assets/script-python.template` — Python script with PEP 723 inline-deps
  block, argparse with help/examples, dry-run support.

## Reference files

- `references/authoring-patterns.md` — The agentskills.io "best practices"
  page condensed: gotchas, templates, validation loops, calibrated specificity,
  defaults-not-menus, procedures-over-declarations, plan-validate-execute.
- `references/script-design.md` — The agentskills.io "using scripts" page
  condensed: agentic CLI design, structured output, error message style,
  PEP 723, uvx/npx/pipx version pinning, dry-run patterns.
- `references/this-repo-conventions.md` — Conventions specific to *this*
  repository: where to put local vs vendor skills, how the 5-level skill
  search works, AGENTS.md ↔ CLAUDE.md sync, where mirrored scripts live.

## Gotchas

- **AGENTS.md is a symlink to CLAUDE.md** — edit either one; never replace the
  symlink with a real file.
- **Skill discovery is one level deep first, then recursive up to 5 levels.**
  `skills/local/<name>/SKILL.md` works because of the recursive fallback. Don't
  nest skills more than 5 deep or they become invisible.
- **`bash 3.2` compatibility** is required for any script that might run on
  stock macOS. No `mapfile`, no `${var,,}` lowercasing, no `[[ -v var ]]`.
  See `references/script-design.md` for the safe subset.
- **`description` is always-on context and has agent-specific hard limits.**
  Put concrete trigger phrases in frontmatter, but keep local skills in the
  120-500 char preferred range when possible. Treat >1024 chars as invalid:
  Codex and Cursor/spec-aligned validators can skip the skill entirely.
- **Quote any `description` containing `:`, `#`, or leading punctuation.** An
  unquoted YAML plain scalar cannot contain `": "` — `npx skills` fails with
  "Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings" and drops the skill
  from the picker without a non-zero exit. ` #` is worse: it parses, but YAML
  treats the rest as a comment and silently truncates your trigger string.
  Single quotes need no escaping except `'` itself. Run
  `scripts/lint-frontmatter.sh` to catch both; see
  `pitfalls/skill-description-colon-breaks-yaml-frontmatter.md` in this repo.
- **Don't write a skill that wraps something the agent already does well.**
  If a stock Claude session handles the task in one turn without help, a skill
  adds context-window cost for no gain. Test the no-skill baseline before
  investing in authoring.
- **Scope auto-detect can surprise you.** `new-skill.sh` walks up looking for
  a publishing-repo anchor (`vendor.yaml` / `skills/local/` /
  `skills/.claude-plugin/`) *first*, then a `.git`. If you ran it from inside
  a clone of this repo while meaning to add a skill to your *other* project,
  it'll silently land in `skills/local/`. Pass `--project` or `--global`
  explicitly when intent isn't obvious, and prefer asking the user
  system-wide-vs-project-wide before running.
- **Discovery symlinks must be `../../`-relative**, not repo-root-relative —
  POSIX resolves symlink targets relative to the link's own directory. The
  script enforces this and verifies each link with `test -e <link>/SKILL.md`;
  if you ever hand-create one, see
  [`pitfalls/symlink-target-relative-to-symlink-not-cwd.md`](../../../pitfalls/symlink-target-relative-to-symlink-not-cwd.md).

## When the user is updating an existing skill (not creating new)

Same workflow, but skip step 2 (scaffold). Read the existing SKILL.md first,
identify which patterns from `references/authoring-patterns.md` are missing or
weakly applied, and propose edits one section at a time so the user can sanity
check. After edits, run lint, then offer the `skill-creator` handoff for
quantitative validation.

# forge-native-dev

An opinionated, issue-driven development workflow that treats GitHub/GitLab as
the single source of truth for intent, backlog, and collaboration — not just
code hosting.

**Core thesis**: Issues are the unit of work. PRs are review gates. With AI
agents, creating a PR is near-zero cost — the human's job shifts from
*proposing* changes (PR-first) to *describing intent* (issue-first) and
*reviewing* results (PR-as-gate).

Lifecycle: **Issue -> branch -> worktree -> work -> PR -> review -> merge -> cleanup**.

Surfaces, separated by the question they answer:

| Surface | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| `references/issue-driven-workflow.md` | "Why issues over local TODO.md?" |
| `references/forge-abstraction.md` | "What `gh` command maps to what `glab` command?" |
| `references/agent-patterns.md` | "How do I wire agents to work from issues?" |
| `references/coexistence.md` | "I have git-workflow / PKH installed too — which wins?" |
| `references/github-features.md` | "How do I use Discussions, Projects, Wiki?" |
| `references/gitlab-features.md` | "How do I use Boards, Threads, CI/CD?" |
| `references/conventions.md` | "What commit/branch/merge conventions should I follow?" |
| `scripts/forge.sh` | The sourced library — all other scripts depend on it. |
| `scripts/forge-init.sh` | One-shot repo setup. |
| `scripts/forge-worktree.sh` | Issue-to-worktree-to-PR lifecycle. |
| `scripts/forge-cleanup.sh` | Auto-cleanup merged branches + worktrees. |
| `scripts/forge-status.sh` | Alignment dashboard. |
| `scripts/forge-issue.sh` | Standalone issue operations. |
| `scripts/forge-pr.sh` | Standalone PR/MR operations. |

## When to use this skill

- The user says "open an issue", "create a backlog item", "開 issue",
  "maybe later", "先記下來", or describes a bug/idea worth tracking.
- The user asks "should I open a PR?", "幫我開 PR", or finishes work on
  a branch and needs to ship it.
- The user says "clean up branches", "清理 branch", "which branches are
  done?", or has stale worktrees.
- The user wants to see the state of their issues/branches/PRs at a glance.
- A new project needs to be set up for issue-driven development.
- The user asks about configuring agents to work from GitHub/GitLab issues.

## When NOT to use this skill

- The project has no GitHub/GitLab remote — use `git-workflow` instead.
- The user explicitly prefers `project-knowledge-harness` (local TODO.md).
- Purely offline git operations with no forge interaction.
- Secret scanning or agent transcript hygiene — use `agent-history-hygiene`.

## Coexistence with other skills

### If `git-workflow` is also installed

Both skills cover branching, PRs, and worktrees. On first ambiguous
operation (e.g., "should I branch?", "open a PR"), ask the user:

> I see both `git-workflow` (git-native) and `forge-native-dev`
> (GitHub/GitLab-native) are available. Which workflow do you prefer for
> this project? Default: `forge-native-dev` for any operation involving
> the remote forge.

Once decided, remember the preference for the session. `forge-native-dev`
is the upgrade path — it covers everything `git-workflow` does plus the
forge layer.

### If `project-knowledge-harness` is also installed

PKH uses `TODO.md` + `backlog/` + `pitfalls/` as file-based project memory.
`forge-native-dev` uses Issues + Discussions + in-repo `pitfalls/`.

If `TODO.md` exists with PKH markers (`## P1` / `## P2` etc.), warn:

> This project uses `project-knowledge-harness` (local TODO.md) for backlog.
> `forge-native-dev` uses Issues instead. Using both creates duplicate
> sources of truth. Which do you prefer for this project?

**One workflow per project, not both.** The migration path is documented in
[`references/coexistence.md`](references/coexistence.md).

## Core workflow

### 1. Setup (once per project)

```bash
bash scripts/forge-init.sh --target /path/to/project --project-name "My Project"
```

This detects the forge, creates labels, configures git, and adds agent
guidance to `AGENTS.md`. Read [`references/forge-abstraction.md`](references/forge-abstraction.md)
for the full gh/glab mapping.

### 2. Capture intent as Issues

When the user surfaces a "maybe later" idea, a bug, or a feature request:

**Default to creating an Issue.** Do not ask "should I create an issue?" —
just create it with appropriate labels.

```bash
# Quick backlog item
bash scripts/forge-issue.sh backlog \
  --title "Add pagination to search" \
  --body "Results page loads all items; should paginate at 50." \
  --priority P3 --effort M

# Bug report
bash scripts/forge-issue.sh create \
  --title "Login redirect fails on Safari" \
  --body "Steps to reproduce: ..." \
  --label "type/bug" --label "priority/P2"

# Feature request
bash scripts/forge-issue.sh create \
  --title "Add dark mode toggle" \
  --body "User preference, persist in localStorage." \
  --label "type/feature" --label "backlog"
```

### 3. Work on an issue

```bash
# Start: creates branch + worktree, assigns issue, adds "in-progress" label
bash scripts/forge-worktree.sh start 42

# Agent variant (uses agent/ branch prefix)
bash scripts/forge-worktree.sh --agent start 42

# Work in the worktree
cd .worktrees/issue-42/
# ... make changes, commit conventionally ...

# Finish: pushes branch, creates PR linking to issue
bash scripts/forge-worktree.sh finish 42
```

### 4. Review and merge

The PR is a review artifact. The issue already described the intent.
PR description auto-fills with `Closes #42`.

Review happens on the PR — by humans, review agents, or both.

```bash
# Check PR status
bash scripts/forge-pr.sh status

# Merge (default: squash, delete branch)
bash scripts/forge-pr.sh merge 55
```

### 5. Clean up

After PRs merge, clean up stale branches and worktrees:

```bash
# See what's ready to clean
bash scripts/forge-cleanup.sh --dry-run

# Clean with confirmation
bash scripts/forge-cleanup.sh

# Force (no confirmation, for scripted use)
bash scripts/forge-cleanup.sh --force
```

### 6. Dashboard

See the full state at a glance:

```bash
bash scripts/forge-status.sh          # your assigned issues
bash scripts/forge-status.sh --all    # all open issues
```

## Merge strategy

**Default: squash and merge.** One issue = one PR = one commit on `main`.

| Strategy | When to use |
|---|---|
| **Squash and merge** | Default. Agent/vibe-coding PRs with WIP commits. Gives the cleanest `git log`. |
| **Rebase and merge** | Every commit in the PR is a meaningful, curated logical change worth preserving. |
| **Create a merge commit** | Almost never in this workflow. Only if you need branch topology in history. |

Why squash is the default:
- Agent work produces noisy WIP commits — squash collapses them into one clean commit.
- One commit per issue on `main` makes `git log --oneline` a readable changelog.
- The squash commit message carries `Closes #N`, auto-closing the issue.
- `git bisect` and `git revert` operate on meaningful units (one feature/fix).

`forge-pr.sh merge` defaults to `--squash`. Override with `--rebase` when
commits are curated, or `--merge` when you need the topology (rare).

## Role awareness

The skill detects your access level to decide what operations are available:

| Role | Detection | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **Maintainer** | Has push/write access (owner, org dev with write, collaborator) | Creates labels, assigns issues, sets priority, merges PRs |
| **Contributor** | Read-only or fork-based | Opens issues/PRs, describes priority in body text, leaves labeling to maintainers |

Detection is automatic via `forge_detect_role` (queries repo permissions API).
Override with `--role maintainer` or `--role contributor` in `forge-init.sh`,
or set `FORGE_ROLE_OVERRIDE=maintainer` / `FORGE_ROLE_OVERRIDE=contributor`
in your shell.

### Maintainer behavior

- `forge-init.sh` creates labels, scaffolds issue templates
- `forge-issue.sh backlog` applies `priority/*` and `backlog` labels directly
- `forge-worktree.sh start` assigns the issue and adds `in-progress` label
- Full access to merge, close, and triage

### Contributor behavior

- `forge-init.sh` skips label creation (labels are managed by maintainers)
- `forge-issue.sh backlog` notes priority in the issue body as a suggestion,
  does not apply labels (maintainer will triage)
- Issue templates are still scaffolded (they're just files in the repo)
- PRs can be opened; merging is up to maintainers

**Note**: "maintainer" here means anyone with write access — this includes
org members, collaborators, and core contributors, not just the repo owner.
If you can push to the repo, you're a maintainer in this skill's model.

## Issue vs Discussion: content boundary

| | Issue | Discussion |
|---|---|---|
| **Nature** | Actionable, with clear done criteria | Open-ended: evaluations, trade-offs, "should we?" |
| **Lifecycle** | Open → In Progress → PR → Closed | Open → threaded conversation → may spawn Issue |
| **Signals** | "Fix X", "Add Y", "Build Z" | "Should we use X?", "Compare A vs B", "Evaluate" |
| **Body** | Concise — what to do, acceptance criteria | Detailed — analysis, pros/cons, research |
| **Closing** | Closed when the PR merges | Stays open for ongoing discussion, or answered |

**Promotion pattern**: when a Discussion matures into actionable work,
create an Issue and link back to the Discussion. The Issue body says
"Design decided in Discussion #N — proceeding with approach B."

**Keep issue bodies concise.** Detailed analysis, trade-off tables, and
research belong in Discussion threads or `backlog/` docs, linked from the
issue. An issue cluttered with research is hard to scan for "what do I
need to build?"

**Cross-referencing**: Issues, Discussions, and PRs can all reference each
other via `#N`. Use this freely — the three-way linking is the key value
of using the forge natively.

## Where things go

| Kind of information | Where it lives | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Actionable work (bugs, features, chores) | Issues (with priority labels) | Searchable, assignable, linkable |
| Design discussion, research, trade-offs | GitHub Discussions / GitLab issue threads | Collaborative, threaded |
| Past traps, debugging knowledge | `pitfalls/` in-repo | Grep-able by symptom, portable |
| Code review | PR/MR comments | Tied to the diff |
| Backlog visualization | GitHub Projects / GitLab Boards | Built-in to the forge |
| Release notes | Tags + auto-generated release notes | Derived from PRs |

**Pitfalls stay in-repo** even in forge-native mode. They need to be
grep-able by error message from any clone. Research and discussion go to
the forge because they benefit from collaboration features.

## Issue-as-backlog conventions

Use labels to mirror priority and type:

- `priority/P1`, `priority/P2`, `priority/P3` — priority lanes
- `type/bug`, `type/feature`, `type/chore` — work type
- `backlog` — deferred work (equivalent to PKH's `## P?`)
- `agent-task` — explicitly flagged for agent implementation
- `in-progress` — currently being worked on
- `discussion` — not actionable work, just a topic

## Agent guidance for issue-driven work

### Checking for work

When the user asks "what should I work on?" or "有什麼可以做的?":

```bash
bash scripts/forge-issue.sh list --assignee @me
```

### Progress reporting

When working on a long task, post progress comments on the issue:

```bash
bash scripts/forge-issue.sh comment 42 \
  --body "Progress: implemented the API endpoint, working on tests next."
```

### Multi-session / multi-agent work

Each agent session should work in its own worktree. Use `--agent` prefix
to distinguish agent branches from human branches:

```bash
# Agent 1 works on issue 42
bash scripts/forge-worktree.sh --agent start 42

# Agent 2 works on issue 38
bash scripts/forge-worktree.sh --agent start 38
```

### Agent configuration patterns

See [`references/agent-patterns.md`](references/agent-patterns.md) for
concrete recipes:

- GitHub: Copilot coding agent in issues, GitHub Actions triggers
- Cursor: background agents, worktree-per-issue sessions
- Claude Code: `--worktree` flag, issue-driven sessions

## Branch naming

| Who | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Human | `issue/<number>-<slug>` | `issue/42-add-oauth` |
| Agent | `agent/issue/<number>-<slug>` | `agent/issue/42-add-oauth` |

Both patterns are recognized by `forge-cleanup.sh` and `forge-status.sh`.

## Available scripts

- **`scripts/forge.sh`** — sourced library, not run directly. All other
  scripts depend on it. Exports `forge_detect`, `forge_issue_*`,
  `forge_pr_*`, `forge_label_ensure`, `forge_slugify`, `forge_whoami`,
  `forge_default_branch`.
- **`scripts/forge-init.sh [--target DIR] [--project-name NAME] [--role auto|maintainer|contributor] [--skip-labels] [--skip-templates] [--skip-git-config] [--force] [--help]`**
  — one-shot setup: labels (maintainer only), issue templates, git config,
  AGENTS.md snippet. Role auto-detected from API permissions.
- **`scripts/forge-worktree.sh <start|finish|list> [ISSUE_NUM] [--agent] [--base BRANCH] [--draft] [--help]`**
  — the core lifecycle script.
- **`scripts/forge-cleanup.sh [--dry-run] [--force] [--all] [--help]`**
  — auto-cleanup merged branches + worktrees.
- **`scripts/forge-status.sh [--json] [--assigned] [--all] [--help]`**
  — alignment dashboard.
- **`scripts/forge-issue.sh <create|list|view|close|comment|assign|label|backlog> [--help]`**
  — standalone issue operations.
- **`scripts/forge-pr.sh <create|list|view|status|merge|link> [--help]`**
  — standalone PR/MR operations.

## Gotchas

- **`gh` / `glab` must be installed and authenticated.** The skill degrades
  to error messages without them — it does not fall back to raw git for
  forge operations. Run `gh auth status` or `glab auth status` to verify.
- **Squash-merge orphans the source branch.** After a squashed PR, the
  branch's commits never appear on the base, so `git branch --merged`
  won't list it. `forge-cleanup.sh` handles this by checking PR status
  directly instead of relying on git merge state.
- **Worktree path is relative to repo root.** `FORGE_WORKTREE_ROOT`
  defaults to `.worktrees`. It should be gitignored (the init script does
  this). Gitignored files (`.env`, etc.) are NOT auto-copied into
  worktrees — use a `.worktreeinclude` file (see `git-workflow`'s
  `references/worktrees-parallel-agents.md`).
- **One branch per issue.** If multiple branches match `issue/42-*`, the
  scripts error. Resolve manually or use `--agent` for agent branches.
- **GitHub Discussions API requires GraphQL.** The `forge_discussion_create`
  function falls back to creating a labeled issue. Use the web UI for full
  Discussion features until the CLI catches up.
- **Label creation is idempotent but case-sensitive.** `priority/P1` and
  `Priority/P1` are treated as different labels. Stick with lowercase.
- **Issue templates are scaffolded, not enforced.** The init script copies
  templates into `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` or `.gitlab/issue_templates/`.
  Users can modify or remove them.
- **The `@me` assignee shortcut** works in `gh` but may need the actual
  username in older `glab` versions.
- **After a PR merges, always create a new branch from updated main.**
  Do not reuse the merged branch (squash-merge makes its history diverge
  from main). Do not try to reopen a merged PR (GitHub does not allow it).
  Each PR is one logical change; follow-ups are new branches and new PRs.
  See [`references/conventions.md`](references/conventions.md) for details.
- **GitHub Discussion categories cannot be created via API.** The GraphQL
  API has no `createDiscussionCategory` mutation. Default categories
  (General, Ideas, Q&A, Announcements, Polls, Show and tell) are created
  automatically when Discussions is enabled. Custom categories (e.g.
  "Design", "Research") must be created via the web UI:
  Settings → Discussions → New category.
- **`gh project link --owner @me` fails for personal repos.** Use the
  actual username (e.g. `--owner myuser`) extracted from the remote URL.
  The `forge_project_create` function handles this automatically.

1	# Authoring patterns
2	
3	Condensed from <https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/best-practices>. Read this
4	before writing or editing a SKILL.md body.
5	
6	## Table of contents
7	
8	1. [Spending context wisely](#spending-context-wisely)
9	2. [Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility](#cross-agent-frontmatter-compatibility)
10	3. [Calibrating control](#calibrating-control)
11	4. [Gotchas sections](#gotchas-sections)
12	5. [Output templates](#output-templates)
13	6. [Checklists for multi-step workflows](#checklists-for-multi-step-workflows)
14	7. [Validation loops](#validation-loops)
15	8. [Plan-validate-execute](#plan-validate-execute)
16	9. [Bundling reusable scripts](#bundling-reusable-scripts)
17	10. [Quick checklist before commit](#quick-checklist-before-commit)
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Spending context wisely
22	
23	Every token in `SKILL.md` competes with the conversation history, the system
24	prompt, and every other active skill. Spend tokens on what the agent **wouldn't
25	know without you**:
26	
27	- Project-specific conventions (table names, repo layout, internal jargon)
28	- Domain-specific procedures with non-obvious steps
29	- Edge cases the agent will misjudge by default
30	- Specific tools/APIs to prefer (with the *why*, briefly)
31	
32	Don't spend tokens on:
33	
34	- Explaining what well-known things are (PDF, HTTP, REST, JSON)
35	- Generic "best practices" the agent already applies (handle errors, write tests)
36	- Comprehensive option enumerations — give a default and one escape hatch
37	
38	**Test:** for each paragraph, ask "would the agent get this wrong without it?"
39	If no, cut it.
40	
41	### Progressive disclosure
42	
43	Three loading levels:
44	
45	| Level | Loaded | Budget |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| Frontmatter (`name`, `description`) | always | 120-500 chars preferred, 1024 max |
48	| `SKILL.md` body | when skill triggers | <500 lines, <5000 tokens |
49	| `references/*.md`, `assets/*`, `scripts/*` | on demand | unlimited |
50	
51	If `SKILL.md` is creeping past 500 lines, move sections to `references/<topic>.md`
52	and reference them with **load conditions** ("Read X if Y happens"), not just
53	"see X for details". Conditions let the agent load on demand; bare pointers tend
54	to either get ignored or get pre-loaded out of caution.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Cross-agent frontmatter compatibility
59	
60	Use this as the portable baseline for coding agents that consume Agent Skills:
61	
62	- `name`: required, lowercase letters/digits/hyphens only, no leading/trailing
63	  hyphen, no `--`, <=64 characters.
64	- `description`: required, non-empty string, <=1024 characters. Include both
65	  what the skill does and concrete trigger contexts. Keep the first 60
66	  characters meaningful because `npx skills` truncates picker hints there.
67	- **Quoting**: a YAML plain (unquoted) scalar may not contain `": "`, and ` #`
68	  starts a comment. Long English descriptions hit both constantly
69	  (`"…debug a FastAPI app: choosing def vs async def"`). Wrap such values in
70	  single quotes — the whole skill is otherwise skipped at install time with
71	  "Nested mappings are not allowed in compact mappings", or installs with a
72	  silently truncated description. `scripts/lint-frontmatter.sh` gates this.
73	- Keep `name` and `description` as the only required frontmatter fields for
74	  portability. Agent-specific fields are allowed when needed, but isolate them
75	  intentionally: Cursor uses `disable-model-invocation`, Codex can read
76	  `agents/openai.yaml`, and some vendored skills carry upstream-only metadata.
77	
78	Description budget tiers:
79	
80	| Tier | Length | Meaning |
81	|---|---:|---|
82	| Green | 120-500 chars | Preferred for local skills: enough trigger surface without context bloat |
83	| Yellow | 501-900 chars | Valid, but context-heavy; move details to `SKILL.md` body |
84	| Orange | 901-1024 chars | Valid, but close to hard loader limits |
85	| Red | >1024 chars | Invalid for Codex/Cursor/spec-aligned validators |
86	
87	Agent notes:
88	
89	- **Codex** skips invalid `SKILL.md` files; OpenAI's validator enforces the
90	  64-char name and 1024-char description limits.
91	- **Cursor** managed `create-skill` guidance matches the same 64/1024 limits
92	  and supports `disable-model-invocation` for explicit-only skills.
93	- **Claude Code** uses descriptions for discovery and tolerates additional
94	  frontmatter in practice, but long descriptions still consume always-on
95	  context and are poor picker hints.
96	- **OpenCode** follows the Agent Skills convention and uses descriptions for
97	  invocation; stay within the portable baseline unless a target agent's docs
98	  say otherwise.
99	- **Claude.ai upload** may impose stricter UI limits. Treat that as a separate
100	  packaging target, not the default coding-agent baseline for this repo.
101	
102	---
103	
104	## Calibrating control
105	
106	Match instruction specificity to **task fragility**, not to "we should be thorough".
107	
108	### Be prescriptive when:
109	
110	- The operation is destructive or has side effects
111	- A specific sequence of steps must hold (migration, release, deploy)
112	- An external system requires exact format (API contract, parser input)
113	
114	```markdown
115	## Database migration
116	
117	Run exactly this sequence:
118	
119	    python scripts/migrate.py --verify --backup
120	
121	Do not modify the command or add flags. The `--verify` step seeds an
122	integrity check that later phases depend on.
123	```
124	
125	The trailing sentence is the trick — even when prescriptive, **explain why**.
126	Agents that understand the reason follow it more reliably than agents that just
127	see "DO NOT" in caps.
128	
129	### Give the agent freedom when:
130	
131	- Multiple valid approaches exist
132	- The output is judgment-driven (code review, refactor proposal)
133	- You'd be hand-coding policy if you wrote it all out
134	
135	```markdown
136	## Code review process
137	
138	1. Check database queries for SQL injection (use parameterized queries)
139	2. Verify auth checks on every endpoint
140	3. Look for race conditions in concurrent code paths
141	4. Confirm error messages don't leak internals
142	```
143	
144	Notice: *what to look for*, not *how to look for it*. The agent picks the
145	approach.
146	
147	### Defaults, not menus
148	
149	When several tools could work, pick one default and mention alternatives as
150	escape hatches.
151	
152	```markdown
153	Use pdfplumber for text extraction.
154	
155	For scanned PDFs requiring OCR, fall back to pdf2image with pytesseract.
156	```
157	
158	…not:
159	
160	```markdown
161	You can use pypdf, pdfplumber, PyMuPDF, or pdf2image depending on...
162	```
163	
164	### Procedures over declarations
165	
166	Teach the agent *how* to approach the class of problem, not *what* to produce
167	for one instance.
168	
169	```markdown
170	Bad — only useful for this exact query:
171	  Join `orders` to `customers` on `customer_id`, filter region='EMEA',
172	  sum `amount`.
173	
174	Good — works for any query:
175	  1. Read schema from `references/schema.yaml` to find relevant tables.
176	  2. Join via the `_id` foreign key convention.
177	  3. Apply user-requested filters as WHERE clauses.
178	  4. Aggregate numeric columns and format as a markdown table.
179	```
180	
181	Specifics still belong in the skill (output format templates, "never output
182	PII", tool-specific quirks) — but the *approach* should generalize.
183	
184	---
185	
186	## Gotchas sections
187	
188	Often the single highest-value section in a skill. **Concrete corrections to
189	mistakes the agent will make without being told.** Not generic advice.
190	
191	```markdown
192	## Gotchas
193	
194	- The `users` table uses soft deletes. Queries must include
195	  `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` or results will include deactivated accounts.
196	- The user ID is `user_id` in the database, `uid` in the auth service, and
197	  `accountId` in the billing API. All three refer to the same value.
198	- The `/health` endpoint returns 200 if the web server is up, even if the
199	  database is down. Use `/ready` to check full service health.
200	```
201	
202	Keep gotchas in `SKILL.md`, not in a separate reference. The whole point is
203	that the agent reads them **before** hitting the situation — by the time it
204	realizes it should load `references/gotchas.md`, the bug has happened.
205	
206	**Iteration tip:** every time you correct the agent during a real run, add the
207	correction here. Most skills' gotchas sections grow over weeks, not get written
208	all at once.
209	
210	---
211	
212	## Output templates
213	
214	Agents pattern-match against concrete structures more reliably than they
215	follow prose descriptions. When the output has a fixed shape, paste the shape:
216	
217	````markdown
218	## Report structure
219	
220	Use this template, adapting sections as needed:
221	
222	```markdown
223	# [Analysis Title]
224	
225	## Executive summary
226	[One paragraph]
227	
228	## Key findings
229	- Finding 1 with supporting data
230	- Finding 2 with supporting data
231	
232	## Recommendations
233	1. Specific actionable recommendation
234	2. Specific actionable recommendation
235	```
236	````
237	
238	Long templates or templates that only apply in some cases should live in
239	`assets/<name>.template` and be loaded on demand from `SKILL.md`.
240	
241	---
242	
243	## Checklists for multi-step workflows
244	
245	Make dependencies and validation gates visible:
246	
247	```markdown
248	## Form processing workflow
249	
250	Progress:
251	- [ ] 1. Analyze the form  → `scripts/analyze_form.py`
252	- [ ] 2. Create field mapping  → edit `fields.json`
253	- [ ] 3. Validate mapping  → `scripts/validate_fields.py`
254	- [ ] 4. Fill the form  → `scripts/fill_form.py`
255	- [ ] 5. Verify output  → `scripts/verify_output.py`
256	```
257	
258	The agent treats the checkboxes as state and won't skip to step 4 without
259	ticking 1-3. Dependency arrows make the wiring explicit.
260	
261	---
262	
263	## Validation loops
264	
265	For tasks where output quality is testable, instruct the agent to validate
266	and re-try, not "do your best and stop":
267	
268	```markdown
269	## Editing workflow
270	
271	1. Make your edits.
272	2. Run validation: `python scripts/validate.py output/`
273	3. If validation fails:
274	   - Read the error message.
275	   - Fix the issues.
276	   - Run validation again.
277	4. Only proceed when validation [REDACTED:generic-credential-uri]es.
278	```
279	
280	The validator can be a script, a reference checklist, or a self-check prompt.
281	The pattern is identical: **do → validate → fix → re-validate → proceed**.
282	
283	---
284	
285	## Plan-validate-execute
286	
287	For batch or destructive operations, force the agent through an intermediate
288	**plan artifact** that gets validated before any side effects happen:
289	
290	```markdown
291	## PDF form filling
292	
293	1. Extract form fields:
294	   `python scripts/analyze_form.py input.pdf`  → `form_fields.json`
295	2. Create `field_values.json` mapping each field name to its intended value.
296	3. Validate:
297	   `python scripts/validate_fields.py form_fields.json field_values.json`
298	   (checks every field exists, types match, required fields present)
299	4. If validation fails, revise `field_values.json` and re-validate.
300	5. Fill the form:
301	   `python scripts/fill_form.py input.pdf field_values.json output.pdf`
302	```
303	
304	The magic is step 3. A validator that catches "field 'signature_date' not
305	found — available: customer_name, order_total, signature_date_signed" lets the
306	agent self-correct **before** the destructive step 5.
307	
308	This pattern eliminates an entire class of "oops, ran the wrong thing on prod"
309	failures. Use it any time the actual operation is hard to undo.
310	
311	---
312	
313	## Bundling reusable scripts
314	
315	When you iterate on a skill (with `skill-creator`), watch the agent transcripts
316	across test runs. If the agent independently reinvents the same logic each run
317	— building the same chart, parsing the same format, validating the same way —
318	that's a signal to write the script once and bundle it in `scripts/`.
319	
320	Heuristic: if you see the same ~20-line helper appearing in 2+ runs, bundle it.
321	
322	See `references/script-design.md` for **how** to design bundled scripts so an
323	agent can call them reliably.
324	
325	---
326	
327	## Quick checklist before commit
328	
329	Before considering a SKILL.md "done":
330	
331	- [ ] Description includes specific trigger contexts ("use when X, Y, Z"),
332	      not just a one-line summary
333	- [ ] Description is "pushy" but within budget: 120-500 chars preferred,
334	      <=1024 chars required
335	- [ ] First 60 description chars are useful in picker UIs
336	- [ ] Name is hyphen-case and <=64 chars
337	- [ ] SKILL.md is under 500 lines (move overflow into `references/`)
338	- [ ] Every `references/*.md` is mentioned with a load condition, not just
339	      listed at the bottom
340	- [ ] Has a `## Gotchas` section (or an honest reason it's empty)
341	- [ ] Output format, if structured, is shown as a literal template
342	- [ ] Multi-step procedures use checklists with dependencies marked
343	- [ ] Destructive operations go through plan-validate-execute or have
344	      `--dry-run` support
345	- [ ] Bundled scripts are listed under `## Available scripts` with their flags
346	- [ ] No "MUST" / "ALWAYS" / "NEVER" in caps without an accompanying *why*
347
`````

1	# Script design for agent skills
2	
3	Condensed from <https://agentskills.io/skill-creation/using-scripts>. Read this
4	before adding anything to `scripts/` in a skill.
5	
6	The headline difference from "regular" CLI design: **the caller is an LLM that
7	reads your stderr to decide what to do next.** Optimize for that.
8	
9	## Table of contents
10	
11	1. [One-off commands vs bundled scripts](#one-off-commands-vs-bundled-scripts)
12	2. [Pin versions for `uvx` / `npx` / `pipx`](#pin-versions)
13	3. [Self-contained scripts (PEP 723 etc.)](#self-contained-scripts)
14	4. [Agentic CLI design rules](#agentic-cli-design-rules)
15	5. [Error message style](#error-message-style)
16	6. [Structured output](#structured-output)
17	7. [Idempotency, dry-run, exit codes](#idempotency-dry-run-exit-codes)
18	8. [Bash 3.2 compatibility (macOS)](#bash-32-compatibility-macos)
19	9. [Quick script checklist](#quick-script-checklist)
20	
21	---
22	
23	## One-off commands vs bundled scripts
24	
25	If a published tool already does the job and the invocation is short, **don't
26	bundle a script** — reference the tool directly:
27	
28	```bash
29	uvx ruff@0.8.0 check .
30	npx eslint@9.0.0 --fix .
31	```
32	
33	Bundle a script when:
34	
35	- The invocation grows past ~3 flags or needs computed arguments.
36	- You need to compose multiple tools.
37	- The logic must be tested independently.
38	- You want to give the agent a stable interface even if the underlying tool
39	  changes.
40	
41	State runtime prerequisites in `SKILL.md` ("Requires Node 18+", "Requires
42	`uv`"). Don't assume the agent's environment.
43	
44	---
45	
46	## Pin versions
47	
48	Unpinned `uvx`, `npx`, `pipx` invocations behave inconsistently as upstreams
49	release new versions. Always pin:
50	
51	```bash
52	# Good
53	uvx ruff@0.8.0 check .
54	npx eslint@9.0.0 --fix .
55	pipx run 'black==24.10.0' .
56	
57	# Bad — silently breaks when upstream ships a breaking change
58	uvx ruff check .
59	npx eslint --fix .
60	```
61	
62	`@latest` is fine **if** the skill explicitly says "tracks upstream latest" and
63	the user understands that.
64	
65	---
66	
67	## Self-contained scripts
68	
69	When a script needs dependencies, prefer **inline declarations** over a
70	sibling `requirements.txt` / `package.json`. The agent can run the script with
71	one command and no setup.
72	
73	### Python — PEP 723
74	
75	```python
76	#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
77	# /// script
78	# requires-python = ">=3.11"
79	# dependencies = [
80	#   "beautifulsoup4>=4.12,<5",
81	# ]
82	# ///
83	"""Extract <p class="info"> from an HTML file."""
84	import sys
85	from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
86	
87	with open(sys.argv[1]) as f:
88	    html = f.read()
89	print(BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser").select_one("p.info").get_text())
90	```
91	
92	Run with `uv run scripts/extract.py file.html`. `uv` creates an isolated
93	environment, installs declared deps, and runs — every time, deterministically.
94	
95	For full reproducibility, `uv lock --script scripts/extract.py` produces
96	`scripts/extract.py.lock`.
97	
98	### Deno
99	
100	```typescript
101	#!/usr/bin/env -S deno run
102	import * as cheerio from "npm:cheerio@1.0.0";
103	// ...
104	```
105	
106	### Bun
107	
108	```typescript
109	#!/usr/bin/env bun
110	import * as cheerio from "cheerio@1.0.0";
111	// ...
112	```
113	
114	If a `node_modules/` exists anywhere up the tree, Bun's auto-install is
115	disabled. Mention this in the skill if relevant.
116	
117	### Ruby
118	
119	```ruby
120	require 'bundler/inline'
121	gemfile do
122	  source 'https://rubygems.org'
123	  gem 'nokogiri', '~> 1.16'
124	end
125	# ...
126	```
127	
128	---
129	
130	## Agentic CLI design rules
131	
132	### No interactive prompts, ever
133	
134	Agents run in non-interactive shells. A script that calls `read`, `input()`,
135	or any TTY prompt **hangs indefinitely**. There is no recovery.
136	
137	```
138	# Bad
139	$ python scripts/deploy.py
140	Target environment: _
141	
142	# Good
143	$ python scripts/deploy.py
144	Error: --env is required. Options: development, staging, production.
145	Usage: python scripts/deploy.py --env staging --tag v1.2.3
146	```
147	
148	Accept all input via flags, env vars, or stdin (non-blocking — check `isatty`).
149	
150	### `--help` is the primary documentation
151	
152	The agent reads `--help` to learn the script. Make it concise but complete:
153	
154	```
155	Usage: scripts/process.py [OPTIONS] INPUT_FILE
156	
157	Process input data and produce a summary report.
158	
159	Options:
160	  --format FORMAT    Output format: json, csv, table (default: json)
161	  --output FILE      Write output to FILE instead of stdout
162	  --verbose          Print progress to stderr
163	  --dry-run          Show what would happen without doing it
164	
165	Examples:
166	  scripts/process.py data.csv
167	  scripts/process.py --format csv --output report.csv data.csv
168	
169	Exit codes:
170	  0  success
171	  1  invalid arguments
172	  2  input file not found
173	  3  processing failed
174	```
175	
176	The exit-codes block matters — the agent uses them to branch retry behavior.
177	
178	---
179	
180	## Error message style
181	
182	When an agent gets an error, the message **directly shapes its next attempt**.
183	Opaque errors waste turns.
184	
185	```
186	# Bad
187	Error: invalid input
188	
189	# Good
190	Error: --format must be one of: json, csv, table.
191	       Received: "xml"
192	```
193	
194	Pattern: **what was wrong + what was expected + what to try.**
195	
196	For "field not found" style errors, include the available alternatives in the
197	message — this lets the agent self-correct without re-querying the system:
198	
199	```
200	Error: Field 'signature_date' not found.
201	       Available fields: customer_name, order_total, signature_date_signed.
202	```
203	
204	---
205	
206	## Structured output
207	
208	Prefer JSON / CSV / TSV / NDJSON over whitespace-aligned columns. Structured
209	output is parseable by both the agent and standard tools (`jq`, `cut`, `awk`).
210	
211	```
212	# Bad
213	NAME          STATUS    CREATED
214	my-service    running   2025-01-15
215	
216	# Good
217	{"name": "my-service", "status": "running", "created": "2025-01-15"}
218	```
219	
220	**Separate data from diagnostics.** Send structured data to stdout; send
221	progress, warnings, debug logs to stderr. The agent can then `jq` stdout
222	cleanly while still seeing diagnostics if it wants.
223	
224	Bash convention:
225	
226	```bash
227	log() { printf '%s\n' "$*" >&2; }   # diagnostics → stderr
228	log "Loading config from $CONFIG"
229	printf '{"status":"ok"}\n'           # data → stdout
230	```
231	
232	---
233	
234	## Idempotency, dry-run, exit codes
235	
236	### Idempotency
237	
238	Agents retry. "Create if not exists" beats "create and fail on duplicate".
239	"Apply migration if not applied" beats "apply migration".
240	
241	### `--dry-run`
242	
243	For destructive or stateful operations, `--dry-run` lets the agent preview
244	and the user confirm. Implement it as a real preview (show what would change),
245	not a no-op:
246	
247	```
248	$ scripts/deploy.sh --dry-run --env staging --tag v1.2.3
249	[dry-run] Would deploy v1.2.3 to staging.
250	[dry-run] Would update 3 services: api, worker, scheduler.
251	[dry-run] Would run post-deploy hook: scripts/healthcheck.sh.
252	```
253	
254	### Exit codes
255	
256	Use distinct codes for distinct failure types. Document them in `--help`.
257	This lets the agent branch retry/recover behavior:
258	
259	| Code | Meaning |
260	|---|---|
261	| 0 | success |
262	| 1 | invalid arguments / usage |
263	| 2 | required input missing or not found |
264	| 3 | external system failure (network, auth, dependency) |
265	| 4 | validation failed |
266	| ≥10 | reserved for skill-specific conditions |
267	
268	### Predictable output size
269	
270	Many agent harnesses truncate tool output past ~10-30K characters. If your
271	script can produce large output:
272	
273	- Default to a summary or a sane limit
274	- Provide `--offset` / `--limit` for pagination
275	- Or require `--output FILE` so the agent has to opt in to stdout
276	
277	---
278	
279	## Bash 3.2 compatibility (macOS)
280	
281	Stock macOS ships bash 3.2. If the script may run on macOS without Homebrew
282	bash, avoid:
283	
284	| Don't use | Use instead |
285	|---|---|
286	| `mapfile -t arr < file` | `while IFS= read -r line; do arr+=("$line"); done < file` |
287	| `${var,,}` (lowercase) | `tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' <<< "$var"` |
288	| `${var^^}` (uppercase) | `tr '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' <<< "$var"` |
289	| `[[ -v VAR ]]` | `[ "${VAR+x}" = "x" ]` |
290	| Associative arrays `declare -A` | indexed array + key parser, or switch to Python |
291	| `wait -n` (wait for any) | `wait` (waits for all) or track PIDs manually |
292	| `&>` redirection | `>file 2>&1` |
293	
294	Lead every script with:
295	
296	```bash
297	#!/usr/bin/env bash
298	set -euo pipefail
299	```
300	
301	`set -u` catches typos in variable names. `set -e` aborts on first error.
302	`set -o pipefail` makes pipelines fail if any stage fails (otherwise only the
303	last stage's exit code matters).
304	
305	If you need bash 4+ features, either:
306	
307	- Switch to Python with PEP 723 (recommended for anything non-trivial).
308	- Add an explicit version check at the top:
309	
310	```bash
311	if (( BASH_VERSINFO[0] < 4 )); then
312	  echo "Error: requires bash >= 4. macOS ships 3.2; install via 'brew install bash'." >&2
313	  exit 1
314	fi
315	```
316	
317	---
318	
319	## Quick script checklist
320	
321	- [ ] Has `#!/usr/bin/env bash` (or equivalent) shebang
322	- [ ] Is `chmod +x`
323	- [ ] Starts with `set -euo pipefail` (bash) or equivalent strict mode
324	- [ ] Responds to `--help` with usage + flags + examples + exit codes
325	- [ ] No interactive prompts; all input via flags / env / stdin
326	- [ ] Errors say *what + expected + try this*
327	- [ ] Data → stdout (structured), diagnostics → stderr
328	- [ ] `--dry-run` for any destructive operation
329	- [ ] Exit codes are distinct and documented
330	- [ ] Pinned versions for any `uvx` / `npx` / `pipx` invocations
331	- [ ] Python helpers use PEP 723 inline deps (not external `requirements.txt`)
332	- [ ] Bash 3.2 compatible if it might run on stock macOS
333	- [ ] Idempotent where possible
334
````

1	# CLAUDE.md

6	## Working with td
7	
8	td keeps task context durable across sessions. In a new context, run `td usage --new-session -q` to see current work.
9	
10	Use your judgment about how much tracking a task needs. For substantive work: `td start <id>`, record progress with `td log`, hand off with `td handoff <id>`, then `td review <id>`.
11	
12	Closing needs a review. Say who did it (default trusted mode; delegated/strict allow only the first):
13	
14	- independent session: `td approve <id> --reason "..."`
15	- a sub-agent: `td approve <id> --reviewed-by "<who>"`
16	- you: `td approve <id> --self-review --reason "..."`
17	
18	Prefer a reviewer with its own `TD_CONTEXT_ID`; never name one who did not review.
19	
20	Run `td usage` or `td <command> --help`.
21	
22	<!-- td-agent-instructions:end -->
23	
24	This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
25	
26	## Project Overview
27	
28	A personal agent skills collection installable via `npx skills@latest add daviddwlee84/agent-skills/skills`. Contains local canonical skills (`skills/local/`), first-party project skills (`skills/owned/`), and cherry-picked third-party skills (`skills/vendor/`). Owned and vendor copies sync from their canonical upstream repos.
29	
30	The skills CLI discovers skills by checking `skills/` one level deep for `SKILL.md`, then falls back to recursive search (up to 5 levels). The nested `local/`/`owned/`/`vendor/` structure works because of this fallback behavior — including vendor `series` subdirs (e.g. `skills/vendor/fullstack-nextjs/<name>/SKILL.md` at depth 4).
31	
32	## Commands
33	
34	```bash
35	# Sync all vendored skills from upstream
36	make sync
37	
38	# Check for upstream updates (dry-run)
39	make sync-check
40	
41	# Validate and render the repo backlog board
42	make kanban
43	
44	# Validate skills/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json (the catalog manifest
45	# that drives the grouped install UI of `npx skills add ...`).
46	make marketplace
47	
48	# Exercise native Claude Code + Codex marketplace add/list/install in isolated state.
49	make native-marketplace-smoke
50	
51	# YAML-parse every skills/**/SKILL.md frontmatter. A file that fails to parse
52	# is silently skipped by `npx skills add` — run this before publishing.
53	make lint-frontmatter
54	
55	# All portable publish gates at once (frontmatter + marketplace + TODO format).
56	# CI additionally runs `make native-marketplace-smoke` with pinned CLIs.
57	make validate
58	
59	# Install scripts/git-hooks/pre-push so `git push` runs `make validate` first.
60	make install-hooks
61	
62	# Add a new vendored skill (auto-syncs)
63	./scripts/add-vendor.sh owner/repo/path/to/skill
64	./scripts/add-vendor.sh https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/branch/path/to/skill
65	# Group under a series subdir (skills/vendor/<series>/<name>/)
66	./scripts/add-vendor.sh --series fullstack-nextjs vercel/vercel-plugin/skills/nextjs
67	
68	# Add a structured TODO entry (preferred over editing TODO.md by hand)
69	./scripts/add-todo.sh --priority P3 --effort M \
70	  --title "Title" --description "Description"
71	
72	# Triage backlog/inbox.md (loose captures) into TODO.md
73	./scripts/sweep-inbox.sh             # interactive
74	./scripts/sweep-inbox.sh --batch     # only formalize parseable key=value lines
75	
76	# Start a TODO item as a td issue (td bridge; no-op without td, TODO.md unchanged)
77	./scripts/start-todo.sh --title "<substring>"
78	
79	# Move an active TODO item to ## Done with the right syntax
80	./scripts/promote-todo.sh --title "<substring>" --summary "<shipped summary>"
81	
82	# Create a new local skill
83	cd skills/local && npx skills@latest init [skill-name]
84	
85	# Docs site (MkDocs Material + llmstxt + copy-to-llm)
86	uv sync --extra docs
87	make docs-serve     # http://127.0.0.1:8000/
88	make docs-build     # produces ./site/
89	```
90	
91	## Source categories and upstream sync
92	
93	- `skills/local/` — canonical skills authored in this repository.
94	- `skills/owned/` — first-party skills maintained in another repository owned by the maintainer. Edit the source project, then sync its distribution copy here.
95	- `skills/vendor/` — third-party upstream skills; preserve upstream content.
96	
97	`vendor.yaml` remains the shared sync manifest. `collection: owned` selects
98	`skills/owned/`; an omitted collection defaults to `vendor`. Both support `series`,
99	`license_path`, `frozen`, and upstream commit tracking. Add published owned sources
100	with `scripts/add-vendor.sh --owned <owner/repo/path>`. A cross-repository symlink
101	cannot serve as a distributable copy.
102	
103	An unpublished owned skill may use `pending_upstream: true`. Its bootstrap mirror
104	contains real files but claims no remote SHA; routine sync/check preserves it.
105	After publishing the canonical source, run `scripts/sync-vendor.sh --activate <name>`.
106	Only a successful sync clears pending. See [owned workflow](docs/workflows/adding-owned-skills.md).
107	
108	## Vendor System (also used for owned sources)
109	
110	- `vendor.yaml` — manifest of upstream skill sources with `last_sync` tracking (date + commit SHA). Optional per-entry `series:` field groups skills under `skills/vendor/<series>/<name>/`; optional `license_path:` copies a repo-level license into the vendored directory as `LICENSE.txt`; entries without `series` stay flat at `skills/vendor/<name>/`
111	- `scripts/sync-vendor.sh` — downloads skill files via GitHub API (`gh` + `yq` required); honors the `series` field for nested destinations, and skips any entry carrying a `frozen:` block (see below)
112	- `scripts/add-vendor.sh` — adds entries to `vendor.yaml`, verifies upstream exists, deduplicates; [REDACTED:generic-credential-uri] `--series <name>` to group into a series subdir
113	
114	Sync uses the git trees API to recursively download skill directories (SKILL.md + references/ etc.) and updates `vendor.yaml` with the latest commit SHA. When `license_path` is present it also tracks the license blob SHA, so a license-only upstream change is visible to `make sync-check`.
115	
116	`.github/workflows/vendor-sync.yml` runs `make sync` weekly (Mon 03:00 UTC,
117	plus `workflow_dispatch` with an optional single-skill filter) and opens/updates
118	a PR on the fixed branch `chore/vendor-sync` — never a direct commit to `main`,
119	because vendored content ships to downstream agents via `npx skills update` and
120	a broken frontmatter is silently skipped rather than erroring. PRs created with
121	`GITHUB_TOKEN` do not trigger `validate.yml`, so the sync job runs the publish
122	gates itself. A red sync job usually means an upstream rename/removal — handle
123	it with `renamed_from:` or `frozen:` as below.
124	
125	Active series in this repo:
126	- `fullstack-nextjs` — Next.js + Supabase + shadcn/ui + Tailwind + design/testing skills (9 skills from vercel/vercel-plugin, vercel-labs/agent-skills, supabase/agent-skills, anthropics/skills)
127	
128	### When an upstream skill is renamed or removed
129	
130	Upstream repos reorganize; `make sync` fails hard if a tracked
131	`upstream.path` no longer exists (the download step finds no files).
132	Handle the two cases explicitly in `vendor.yaml`:
133	
134	- **Renamed upstream** — update `name` + `upstream.path` to the new
135	  values, `git mv` the vendored dir, fix that skill's `skills[]` path in
136	  `marketplace.json`, and add a `renamed_from: <old-name>` field so the
137	  history stays greppable. Renaming changes the *downstream* install id:
138	  `skills@1.5.24` writes `skills-lock.json`, but a renamed skill is still a
139	  different install ID; review the lock and explicitly reinstall the new name.
140	- **Removed upstream** — freeze it with a `frozen:` block (`reason:` +
141	  `since:`). `sync-vendor.sh` then skips the entry in both `make sync`
142	  and `make sync-check` while keeping the last-synced copy and its
143	  `marketplace.json` entry. Don't delete a vendored copy just because
144	  upstream did — unless you also mean to stop shipping it.
145	
146	Live examples in `vendor.yaml`: `diagnosing-bugs` (`renamed_from: diagnose`)
147	and `zoom-out` (`frozen:`), both from the 2026-07-05 mattpocock/skills reorg.
148	
149	## Marketplace Catalog
150	
151	`skills/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` defines the user-facing plugin
152	groupings shown by `npx skills@latest add daviddwlee84/agent-skills/skills`.
153	Located under `skills/` (not repo root) because the `/skills` subpath in
154	the install command makes the CLI read the manifest from
155	`<repo>/skills/.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` — see
156	[`docs/reference/npx-skills-metadata.md`](docs/reference/npx-skills-metadata.md)
157	for the full mechanism.
158	
159	When adding a new skill (local or vendored), also append its path to the
160	matching plugin's `skills[]` array in the manifest, or accept that it
161	will fall through to the **Other** group. Run `make marketplace` after
162	editing — the validator catches broken paths, duplicates, and reserved
163	marketplace names. Path format is `./local/<name>`, `./owned/<name>`, or
164	`./vendor/<name>` (relative to `skills/`, not repo root).
165	
166	**Picker ordering is alphabetical-only.** `npx skills` sorts groups by
167	`plugins[].name` (A→Z) and skills within a group by their `SKILL.md`
168	`name` — the `plugins[]` / `skills[]` array order is ignored. To pin a
169	frequently-used group to the top, prefix its `name` with two digits: this
170	repo pins `01-project-memory`, `02-skill-authoring`, `03-infra-and-docs`,
171	`04-ml-workflow`, `05-notebooks`; the rest stay alphabetical. **These
172	`NN-` prefixes are deliberate — don't strip them.** Full mechanism +
173	within-group caveat in
174	[`docs/reference/npx-skills-metadata.md`](docs/reference/npx-skills-metadata.md).
175	
176	## SKILL.md Format
177	
178	Each skill is a directory containing a `SKILL.md` with YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`) and markdown body with instructions, conventions, and examples. Vendored skills may include `references/` subdirectories.
179	
180	## Local Skill Discovery Symlinks (`.agents/skills/`, `.claude/skills/`)
181	
182	The `.agents/skills/<name>` and `.claude/skills/<name>` entries are
183	**discovery symlinks** that make a skill active in *this* repo's own agent
184	context (Cursor and Claude Code load whatever resolves under those dirs).
185	They are unrelated to distribution — downstream users get skills via
186	`npx skills add ...` + `marketplace.json` regardless of these links.
187	
188	`scripts/new-skill.sh --local` (run by the `skill-author` skill) creates
189	both links automatically. **Only keep them for skills that are genuinely
190	useful while working _on this repo_** — e.g. `skill-author`,
191	`mkdocs-site-bootstrap`. Skills authored here purely for downstream use
192	(e.g. `fastapi-ai-*`, `dvc-ml-workflow`, `mlflow-tracking`) should **not**
193	be symlinked: they would load into every in-repo agent session and just
194	bloat/pollute context without ever being exercised here. The canonical copy
195	under `skills/local/<name>/` is all that's needed for distribution.
196	
197	To author a downstream-only skill without the links, either:
198	
199	```bash
200	# Skip the symlinks at creation time
201	bash skills/local/skill-author/scripts/new-skill.sh --local --no-symlinks <name>
202	
203	# …or remove them afterward
204	rm .agents/skills/<name> .claude/skills/<name>
205	```
206	
207	## Project Memory Workflow
208	
209	<!-- forge-native-dev:guidance -->
210	### Issue-driven workflow (GitHub)
211	
212	This project uses GitHub Issues as the canonical backlog and GitHub
213	Discussions for evaluative/research topics. The `forge-native-dev` skill
214	provides the scripts below.
215	
216	| Information | Lives in | Why |
217	|---|---|---|
218	| Actionable work (bugs, features, chores) | [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/agent-skills/issues) | Searchable, assignable, cross-linkable |
219	| Evaluations, "should we?", research | [Discussions](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/agent-skills/discussions) | Threaded, collaborative |
220	| Research docs, trade-off analysis | `backlog/` | In-repo, diffable, reviewed in PRs |
221	| Past traps, debugging knowledge | `pitfalls/` | Grep-able by symptom, portable |
222	| Backlog visualization | [Project board](https://github.com/users/daviddwlee84/projects/11) | Built-in to the forge |
223	| Historical record | `TODO.md` `## Done` section | In git |
224	
225	**Capture intent as Issues** — when the user describes a bug, idea, or
226	"maybe later" item, create an Issue with appropriate labels. Do not ask
227	"should I create an issue?" — default to creating one.
228	
229	**Work lifecycle:**
230	1. Start: `bash skills/local/forge-native-dev/scripts/forge-worktree.sh start <issue-number>`
231	2. Work in the worktree, commit conventionally
232	3. Finish: `bash skills/local/forge-native-dev/scripts/forge-worktree.sh finish <issue-number>`
233	4. After merge: `bash skills/local/forge-native-dev/scripts/forge-cleanup.sh`
234	
235	**Check for work:** `bash skills/local/forge-native-dev/scripts/forge-issue.sh list --assignee @me`
236	
237	**Dashboard:** `bash skills/local/forge-native-dev/scripts/forge-status.sh`
238	
239	**PRs are review gates, not proposals.** The issue describes intent; the
240	PR is the diff to review. Default merge strategy: **squash and merge**.
241	<!-- forge-native-dev:guidance (end) -->
242	
243	### External skill / MCP / domain / curiosity catalog -> `docs/catalog/`
244	
245	`docs/catalog/` is the vendoring decision log + external-awareness
246	registry, separate from `Skills` (what we ship) and `Reference` (our
247	own conventions). It has four subareas:
248	
249	- `docs/catalog/domains/` — per-domain hub pages (one per professional
250	  domain: Finance, Quant Research, AI/ML Research, Web & Fullstack,
251	  Knowledge Work, Agent Harness). Each hub aggregates local + vendored
252	  + external skills + MCPs relevant to that domain. New hubs copy
253	  [`docs/_snippets/domain-hub-template.md`](docs/_snippets/domain-hub-template.md).
254	- `docs/catalog/skill-collections.md` — single curated index of all
255	  upstream skill collections (Anthropic, Vercel, Supabase, marimo,
256	  Warp Oz, Orchestra-Research, etc.) with status per entry. Replaces
257	  the historical `Collections.md` (kept as a stub).
258	- `docs/catalog/curiosities.md` — docs-only shelf for interesting,
259	  provocative, or highly personal skills that are deliberately excluded
260	  from `vendor.yaml`, marketplace grouping, and routine skill discovery.
261	  Entries use `skipped` with the reason they remain docs-only.
262	- `docs/catalog/mcp/` — MCP wiki, modeled after Karpathy's
263	  [LLM Wiki pattern](docs/reference/llm-wiki-pattern.md). One markdown
264	  file per MCP with required YAML frontmatter
265	  (`name / slug / upstream_url / transport / auth / hosting / domain /
266	  status / license / last_verified`).
267	
268	Every external entry carries a status enum (single source of truth in
269	`docs/_snippets/external-install.md`):
270	
271	| Status | Meaning |
272	|---|---|
273	| `vendored` | In `vendor.yaml` — link to the entry. |
274	| `deferred` | Open `TODO P?` item — link to it. |
275	| `skipped` | Looked at, chose not to vendor — inline reason required. |
276	| `evaluated` | Read but no decision — 1-line note. |
277	| `wishlist` | Surfaced but not yet evaluated — default for fresh discoveries. |
278	
279	Status changes trigger existing scripts:
280	`wishlist → deferred` runs `add-todo.sh`; `deferred → vendored` runs
281	`add-vendor.sh` + optionally `promote-todo.sh`. Full recipe in
282	[`docs/workflows/adding-catalog-entries.md`](docs/workflows/adding-catalog-entries.md).
283	
284	Every published catalog page is bilingual (`*.md` + `*.zh-TW.md`).
285	Snippets and `_template.md` are EN-only by convention.
286	
287	### Past pitfalls -> `pitfalls/`
288	
289	When a debugging session uncovers a non-obvious trap that could realistically be
290	hit again, write `pitfalls/<slug>.md` with:
291	
292	1. The verbatim symptom or error text
293	2. The root cause
294	3. The workaround
295	4. Prevention guidance or the hard invariant that supersedes it
296	
297	Use symptom-first titles so future agents can grep the failure they see, not
298	the explanation they do not know yet.
299
